newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW - CVRD sale seen drawing only two groups.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - CVRD sale seen drawing only two groups.

text.p: Despite strong investor interest, Brazil is unlikely to see more than two consortia bidding at the much-awaited auction of Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD), said Elena Landau, the former coordinator of Brazil's privatization program.

"It is unlikely that more than two consortia will bid for a company of the size of CVRD," said Landau, now working for the Brazil branch of the U.S. brokerage Bear Stearns. "Vale's privatization will require a significant amount of cash and a well-defined shareholders' agreement before the auction takes place."

Landau, who was in charge of the privatization program at the National Development Bank (BNDES) for nearly three years until June 1996, said Vale's sell-off rules force investors to seek partnerships.

The BNDES handles all privatizations in Brazil. In her position at the bank, Landau oversaw the initial stages of the project to privatize CRVD, which in value terms is expected to be the biggest government sell-off ever in Latin America.
In the run-up to the April 29 auction of CRVD's first block of shares, two major Brazilian firms are heading talks with investors to form two consortia to bid for the shares on offer.
Brazil's metal, cement and pulp conglomerate Grupo Votorantim is negotiating with Japan's Nippon Steel after it failed to agree with local private steelmaker CSN on who should head the consortium.
Votorantim's group would also include private bank Banco Safra, Vale's employees and local pension funds.
Meanwhile, CSN, together with private bank Bradesco, is in touch with South Africa's Gencor to be its foreign partner. It is also negotiating with domestic pension funds and Vale's workers.
Minorco the conglomerate controlled by Anglo American and De Beers, said it might make a bid for CVRD but made no comment whether it will join one of the two groups now being formed.

According to Vale's tender documents, no single investor may snap up more than 45 percent of Valecom, the holding company which will be formed with the sale of a 45 percent block of voting shares for some three billion reais in April.
Large competitors, purchasers and traders of iron ore will be limited to a 10 percent individual stake in Valecom's capital.
"The privatization model was designed in such a way that it forces investors to share management," she told Reuters in a interview conducted Monday.
Landau shrugged off concerns over mounting opposition to Vale's privatization.

"It will make it harder for the government but will not prevent the privatization from taking place," she said, noting that BNDES has succeeded in all previous privatizations that were put on hold by court actions.
She also criticized a report by a group of 22 university experts led by physicist Luis Pinguelli Rosa that said CVRD, which was valued at 10.3 billion reais, was undervalued.
The report was prepared for a group of congressmen.
"If they wanted to check the process, they should have hired independent consultants, instead of giving the job to people who are clearly against the privatization concept," she said.
Landau also said Vale's privatization represents a key step in the government's reform plans.
"Vale is a typical mining firm to be run by the private sector. Its sell-off confirms the government's commitment to a major reform."
((--Sao Paulo Newsroom, 5511 2485412))
